To further improve efficiency, LightGBM also employs techniques, such as gradient-based one-sided sampling (GOSS) and exclusive feature bundle (EFB), to maintain the model’s accuracy while reducing the computational effort and the number of features and improving training efficiency. LightGBM offers many advantages, such as faster training speed and efficiency, higher accuracy, lower memory usage, and support for parallel, distributed, and GPU learning, making it capable of handling large-scale data [ 294 ]. Key parameters of LightGBM include the learning rate, number of trees, number of leaves, feature fraction, and bagging fraction. Although the leaf-wise strategy is prone to overfitting, especially with small datasets, the complexity of the model can be controlled, and overfitting can be prevented by setting the max depth parameter to limit the depth of the tree [ 294 ]. Ma et al. [ 303 ] used the LightGBM model for the multi-objective prediction of the Vickers hardness and compressive fracture strain of HEAs, and the R 2  of the model was 0.9, which helped them propose suitable atomic percentages of Al, Nb, and Mo for the design of HEAs with high hardness and ductility. Ding et al. [ 304 ] proposed a main framework based on the LightGBM algorithm to achieve a good prediction of the YS of refractory HEAs at different temperatures, with a coefficient of determination,  R 2 , of 0.961 and a good generalization ability. The experimental validations for their framework using TiTaNbHfNi 0.25  and TiTaNbHfNi 0.5  HEAs, which exhibited YSs of 1230 MPa and 1311 MPa with corresponding prediction errors of 6.3% and 3.7%, respectively, demonstrate the excellent performance of their proposed framework. These application cases demonstrate the high accuracy of the LightGBM’s HEA performance prediction, which helps provide reliable guidance for the design of new HEAs.

sections.heading: Neural Networks Algorithms
paragraphs: The basic unit of an artificial neural network (ANN) is the artificial neuron (known as a node), which mimics the function of a biological neuron by summing up weighted inputs and applying a nonlinear activation function to obtain an output [ 252 ]. ANNs can handle nonlinear relationships, parallel computation, and adaptive learning [ 305 ], and are suitable for performance predictions in HEAs. A typical ANN consists of an input, hidden, and output layer. The input layer acts as an entry point to the network and receives external input data. One or more hidden layers perform nonlinear transformations on the input data to learn potential features of the data. The output layer obtains the output of the last hidden layer and generates the final prediction, corresponding to the model’s target output. The training process of an ANN involves adjusting the connection weights between neurons to minimize the error between the predicted and actual values, often using loss functions, such as MSE, and optimization algorithms, such as stochastic-gradient descent (SGD) [ 252 ].

Deep-Neural Networks (DNNs)  Early ANNs, also known as shallow-neural networks, usually had only 1–2 hidden layers due to limitations in computational resources and algorithms [ 306 ], as shown in Fig.  9 a [ 252 ]. With the development of algorithms and hardware, ANN architectures containing more hidden layers, i.e., deep-neural networks (DNNs), as presented in Fig.  9 b [ 306 ], have emerged. These multiple hidden layers enable deep learning and significantly improve the learning ability of the model [ 307 ]. DNNs learn more complex nonlinear relationships by modeling high-level abstractions in the data through multiple nonlinear transformations. DNNs often use more advanced activation functions and regularization techniques to overcome severe overfitting problems due to many parameters and thus improve performance [ 306 ]. Fig. 9 Schematic representation of a classical ANN model and of a DNN model with more hidden layers, which demonstrates superior generalization performance.  a  Fully connected ANN with two hidden layers [ 252 ].  b  The architecture of a DNN with more hidden layers [ 306 ]. The predictive hardness  c  and strength  d  results of DNN for the (CuNiMn)-X HEA [ 310 ].  e  A comparison of the performance of the RF and DNN models, with the RF results on the left and the DNN results on the right. The top row shows the  R 2  score, and the bottom row shows the MAE [ 311 ]. Compared to the RF model, the DNN model exhibits significant generalization advantages when trained on higher-order datasets (second and subsequent rows of the heat map matrix)

Neural network modeling has garnered significant attention in HEA predictions in recent years. Vazquez et al. [ 308 ] developed a DNN model for NiCoCrMnFeAlNb HEA systems, utilizing thermodynamic datasets generated by the thermodynamic HTC. The model effectively identified the most frequent phases, achieving an  R 2  value exceeding 0.96. Catal et al. [ 309 ] employed a two-hidden-layer ANN model to predict the strength, hardness, and ductility of HEAs. This model outperformed RF and SVM models, and, combined with experimental validation, successfully identified the TiNbZrTaMoV-HEA series, which exhibits resistance to thermal softening at 800 °C. Tan et al. [ 310 ] proposed a DNN-based alloy design strategy, predicting hardness and strength with  R 2  values of 0.9798 and 0.9440, respectively (Fig.  9 c, d), surpassing the performance of SVR and ANN models. Crucially, they used this strategy to screen and experimentally validate a high-performance HEA from 308 types of novel (CuNiMn)-X alloys, achieving a hardness of 474 HV, a compressive strength of 2322 MPa, and a strain at fracture of 25.20%. Furthermore, the study quantitatively revealed key factors influencing alloy properties, such as hardness, electronegativity difference, nuclear-charge difference, and their respective thresholds. Liu et al. [ 311 ] compared the performance of RF and DNN models in predicting HEA phase scores using a large CALPHAD-generated dataset comprising 480 million data points. While the RF model exhibited higher predictive accuracy for test sets of the same system order, the DNN model demonstrated superior generalization ability in cross-system order predictions, effectively transferring knowledge learned from lower-order systems to higher-order ones. Figure  9 e compares the performance of the RF (left) and DNN (right) models, displaying an  R 2  score (top row) and MAE (bottom row). The DNN model significantly outperformed the RF model in terms of generalization performance when trained on the higher-order dataset (second and subsequent rows of the heatmap matrix). Moreover, the DNN model demonstrated advantages in handling missing data and predicting topologically relevant phase compositions. This study highlights the potential of DNNs in the HEA phase stability prediction, particularly within the CrHfMoNbTaTiVWZr composition space.

Convolutional Neural Network (CNN)  Early ANNs typically used fully connected layers in which the output of each neuron was connected to every neuron in the next layer [ 252 ]. Fully connected networks are feasible for internal databases with limited descriptors. However, larger datasets containing thousands of descriptors and network parameters (e.g., weights) can readily overfit these networks. The sheer number of parameters also results in high computational costs. These drawbacks have driven the development of more sophisticated and efficient ANN architectures, such as the convolutional neural network (CNN) [ 312 ]. CNN architectures typically comprise three-layer types: convolutional, pooling, and fully connected layers. The convolutional layer is at the core of a CNN, which utilizes a set of learnable filters (or kernels) to extract local features from the input data. These filters, which are typically smaller in size than the input data, generate feature maps through convolutional operations that capture key features of the data [ 312 ]. To improve robustness and reduce computational complexity, the pooling layer reduces the dimensionality of these feature maps [ 313 ]. The fully connected layer then flattens the output of the pooling or convolutional layer into a one-dimensional vector. A nonlinear activation function, such as a sigmoid, tan h , or rectified linear unit (ReLU), is often applied after convolutional and fully connected layers to enhance the model’s nonlinear expressiveness [ 314 ,  315 ].

Mirzaee et al. [ 316 ] successfully predicted the elastic constants of the NiCuAuPdPt HEA system using a 3D CNN with the input data of charge densities calculated based on DFT. As shown in Fig.  10 a, the input data to the model have a size of (56, 40, 40, 1) and are processed through a 3 × 3 × 11 3D convolutional layer and a 2 × 2 × 2 maximum pooling layer. The pooled feature maps were flattened and passed to two fully connected layers, ultimately outputting a vector of size 8. The model employed the ReLU activation function. Charge density  xy -plane images corresponding to different  z -values were combined to construct the 3D-input data for the 3D CNN model (Fig.  10 a). The researchers investigated various image resizing strategies to optimize training accuracy and processing time. Wang et al. [ 317 ] developed an ML model combining a thermodynamic model, a DNN, and a customized CNN to predict the mechanical properties of HEAs. As depicted in Fig.  10 b, the CNN’s input space width corresponded to the number of elemental descriptors ( N ), and the height corresponded to the number of elements ( M ), resulting in an output shape of  M  × 1 ×  N . This output was reshaped to  M  ×  N  × 1 to facilitate layer reuse. Compared to DNN, the CNN model had 98.91% fewer parameters, significantly reducing the training burden. The integrated DNN and CNN models successfully predicted the YS [exhibited in Fig.  10 c,  R 2  = 0.866] and UTS (shown in Fig.  10 d,  R 2  = 0.842) of HEAs. ANNs have demonstrated strong capabilities in HEA predictions, but their interpretability remains a challenge. The “black-box” nature of ANNs makes it difficult to understand the physical mechanisms behind their predictions [ 318 ]. In addition, the sparsity of the HEA performance data challenges the training and generalization capabilities of the models. Future research needs to balance model generalization and interpretability to better understand the relationship between the HEA performance and its components and structure [ 81 ]. Fig. 10 a  CNN architecture used in Reference [ 316 ]. Dropout layers between fully connected layers are not shown. The CNN model takes charge-density data with a size of (56, 40, 40, 1) as the input and outputs eight elastic constants after the multilayer 3D convolution and maximum pooling operations. The charge-density  xy -plane images corresponding to different  z -values are combined to construct the 3D data shown on the right, which is used as the input for the 3D CNN model.  b  The model reshapes the output shape to be identical to the input shape. Its layer structure allows a small number of weights to process a large amount of information, and the repeating hidden layers help learn the complex relationships between the input features and the output. It compares the performance of the integrated DNN and CNN models in predicting YS ( c ) and UTS ( d ) data [ 317 ]

Graph-Neural Networks (GNNs)  Inspired by fields such as computer vision, graph-neural networks (GNNs) are finding increasing applications in materials science due to their automated-feature-extraction capabilities. GNNs excel at extracting relevant descriptors from molecular and crystal structures for predicting material properties [ 319 ,  320 ,  321 ,  322 – 323 ]. The core of GNN is the information-diffusion mechanism. A graph, composed of nodes (representing atoms) and edges (representing interactions between atoms), represents the data. Each node possesses an initial feature vector. GNNs learn by iteratively updating these feature vectors based on information aggregated from neighboring nodes. This process continues until the node representations reach a stable state, effectively capturing the structural information encoded in the graph. Compared to traditional feature-engineering-based ML models, GNNs exhibit less sensitivity to the specific choice of atomic descriptors and typically obviate the need for manual-feature derivation [ 324 ]. These advantages allow GNNs to efficiently describe complex materials, offering improved accuracy in property prediction, valuable chemical insights [ 325 ,  326 ], and a faster alternative to solving the computationally demanding Schrödinger equation [ 323 ,  327 ,  328 ]. For instance, Schütt et al. [ 321 ,  329 ] achieved an excellent performance in molecular property prediction using only atomic numbers and atomic coordinates, demonstrating the power of graph structures to capture interatomic interactions effectively. Numerous GNN architectures have been developed for materials property prediction, including SchNet [ 321 ], crystal-graph-convolution-neural network (CGCNN) [ 322 ], MatErials-graph network (MEGNet) [ 324 ], improved-crystal-graph-convolution-neural network (iCGCNN) [ 326 ], atomistic-line-graph-neural network (ALIGNN) [ 327 ], frame-averaging-equivariant-graph-neural network (FAENet) [ 330 ], and self-attention-enhanced-graph-neural network (SA-GNN) [ 331 ,  332 ]. These models represent materials as graphs and use the multilayer graph convolution to update node features, implicitly capturing multi-body interactions. Since many material properties are highly sensitive to structural features like bond angles and local geometric deformations, explicitly incorporating such information is crucial for enhancing model accuracy [ 321 ,  322 ,  324 ]. While GNNs hold immense promises in materials predictions, several key challenges hinder their broader applications, including the dependence of GNN performance on the amount and diversity of training data (with access to high-quality data remaining a significant hurdle, especially for complex systems like HEAs), the often-limited interpretability of GNN models, and the potentially prohibitive computational cost for large systems [ 333 ,  334 ]. To address these limitations, researchers are actively developing more efficient and interpretable GNN architectures. One promising strategy involves focusing on local atomic environments, as exemplified by the local environment (LE) graph-based representation for HEAs (LESets) proposed by Zhang et al. [ 332 ]. This approach enables efficient learning from limited data and offers improved interpretability through an attention mechanism that highlights the contributions of local environments to the overall material properties.

Several recent studies highlight the GNN’s power of focusing on local environments to predict the properties of high-entropy materials. These studies have shown significant benefits in predicting the thermodynamic properties of vacancies in high-entropy metals [ 335 ], oxides [ 336 ,  337 ], and zinc-blende semiconductors [ 338 ]. Manzoor et al. [ 335 ] provided an efficient framework for predicting the vacancy formation energy (Δ E v ) and the migration energy of multi-component alloys. By considering the local chemical environment around atoms, the framework enables the model to predict defect energies of multi-component alloys with high accuracy in the Ni–Fe–Cr–Co–Cu system, even with limited training data. This idea of using simple system data to predict the properties of complex systems provides a reference for the construction of GNN models. Park et al. [ 336 ] employed an ensemble approach, combining CGCNN [ 322 ] and MEGNet [ 324 ] to predict the Δ E v  in metal oxides. This integration effectively explores the chemical space, spanning binary to quintuple oxides, with improved accuracy when model predictions converge (Δ E v  < 0.5 eV), validating against DFT calculations. These works highlight the power of ensemble GNNs in exploring vast chemical spaces. Witman et al. [ 337 ] introduced the defect-graph-neural network (dGNN), specifically designed for predicting vacancy formation enthalpies (Δ H d ). The dGNN model predicts the Δ H d  directly from the ideal-crystal structure without the need for time-consuming DFT supercell relaxation calculations, which significantly improves the prediction efficiency and the accuracy of prediction. Trained on a dataset of ~ 1500 defect sites across over 200 oxides, the dGNN has successfully screened materials for high-temperature clean energy applications. These studies underscore the potential of GNNs and related ML approaches for accelerating Δ E v  calculations, a critical aspect of investigating oxidation and corrosion resistance in HEAs. These ongoing researches into efficient architecture and improved understanding of GNN decision-making processes promise to further enhance their impact on HEAs.

sections.heading: Unsupervised-Learning Algorithms
paragraphs: Unsupervised learning enables algorithms to learn primarily from an input data structure rather than through explicit instruction for a specific task [ 339 ]. It is a learning paradigm where no labeled data are provided for supervision during training. The objective is to uncover inherent structures and relationships within the data [ 340 ]. In unsupervised learning, the algorithm receives unlabeled datasets and attempts to identify patterns, such as clusters, reduced dimensionality representations, or association rules [ 341 ]. For HEAs, unsupervised-learning algorithms commonly include: (1) Clustering algorithms (e.g., k-means): The k-means algorithm is intended to divide the data into k clusters, where k is a pre-defined hyperparameter. Each data point is iteratively assigned to the cluster whose center,  c k , is most similar, based on a chosen similarity measure [ 342 ]. (2) Subspace analysis techniques (e.g., PCA and t-SNE): PCA is a dimensionality-reduction technique that is implemented by projecting high-dimensional data into a low-dimensional space while preserving as much of its variance as possible [ 343 ]. PCA achieves this result by identifying the directions of the most significant variance within the data (principal components) [ 344 ]. It is frequently employed in data preprocessing to eliminate the redundant information between variables and prepare data for subsequent regression or cluster analysis [ 345 ,  346 ]. The t-SNE is also a dimensionality-reduction technique that models the similarity of data points in the high-dimensional space as a Gaussian distribution, while in the low-dimensional space, it is modeled using the t-distribution [ 223 ]. This approach reduces dimensionality while preserving local structures and global data relationships [ 70 ]. (3) ANN-based algorithms: Unsupervised ANNs can learn complex nonlinear relationships in the HEA data and are valid for feature extraction, noise reduction, and anomaly detection. Specific ANN architectures, such as self-organizing maps (SOMs), are well-suited for unsupervised learning with unlabeled data. SOMs operate on the principle of topological competition between neurons [ 347 ]. The neurons are arranged in a grid (as shown in Fig.  11 c) [ 348 ], each associated with an n-dimensional weight vector. The neuron whose weight vector is closest to a given input vector is designated the “winner.” For each input vector, neurons compete to become the “winner.” The weight vectors of the “winner” and its neighbors are then adjusted to be closer to the input vector [ 349 ]. This competitive learning process allows SOMs to map similar input vectors to neighboring neurons, facilitating data clustering and visualization. SOMs can identify clusters as an unsupervised method but do not directly assign category labels to these clusters [ 262 ]. This unsupervised approach can be used for feature extraction, noise reduction, anomaly detection, and revealing complex nonlinear relationships. Fig. 11 a  The visualization results after downscaling the HEA data to a 2D space by t-SNE are shown and colored according to different labels, in order: coloring based on the hardness label, which is classified into three levels: low (below 400 HV), medium (400–700 HV), and high (above 700 HV); coloring based on the phase-structure label; and coloring based on the k-mean clustering results.  b  Results of SHAP values for the cluster on the left, middle (characterized by high hardness), and right (characterized by single-phase BCC structures) show the effect of Mn and Nb concentrations on the hardness and phase structures [ 350 ].  c  The organization of the input data and the SOM neurons [ 348 ]. Ideally, different categories of data will form clear boundaries in the SOM, as presented in  d . The intensity of the colors in  e  indicates the distance of the weight vectors between the neurons, the darker the color, the greater the distance.  f  (Hits plot) shows the number of data samples associated with each neuron. For example, the number 5 in the upper left corner indicates that the neuron contains 5 data points [ 262 ]

Pan et al. [ 350 ] analyzed the dataset distribution using two-dimensional t-SNE dimensionality reduction and k-means clustering ( k  = 3) (Fig.  11 a). The first two subfigures depict the dimensionality-reduction results based on hardness and phase labels. The third sub-figure shows the k-means clustering results by grouping the data points into three clusters based on phase structures and hardness distributions: “left,” “center,” and “right.” The SHAP values were calculated for the clustered samples (Fig.  11 b). Results indicate that the Mn concentration significantly influences the intermediate, high-hardness cluster, particularly at a low Mn content. Conversely, the Nb concentration is crucial for the right-hand cluster, characterized by a single BCC structure (the third sub-figure in Fig.  11 b), although its effect is opposite to that of Mn. Combining the cluster analysis and SHAP analysis helped reveal potential mechanisms affecting hardness and phase structures. The fact that high-hardness samples are mainly labeled as “other” suggests that the phase structure in a high-hardness HEA may be more complex than a simple FCC or BCC single-phase structure. Comparing predicted and experimental hardness for the AlTiZrHf HEA system further validates this interpretable dimensionality-reduction method for data mining. Huang et al. [ 262 ] analyzed the phase structure of 401 HEAs, including SS, IM, and two-phase mixtures (SS + IM), utilizing SOM (the ideal organizational schematic shown in Fig.  11 c). Figure  11 d depicts an idealized SOM clustering scenario with distinct spatial boundaries separating the SS, IM, and SS + IM phases. The authors visualized the distribution of 401 kinds of alloys in five dimensions, as shown in Fig.  11 e, with the SOM projecting this five-dimensional space onto a two-dimensional plane. Darker regions indicate more excellent neuron proximity and, consequently, higher compositional similarity between alloys. The hits plot (Fig.  11 f) displays the number of alloys associated with each neuron, highlighting the relative concentration of IM phases within the compositional space, and revealing clear boundaries based on the proximity of group-member counts to the number of IM alloys. The high-accuracy prediction of HEA phase structures and properties through an unsupervised learning paradigm demonstrates the method’s potential to reveal composition-structure–property relationships.

sections.heading: Semi-supervised Learning
paragraphs: Based on supervised learning (predicting with the labeled data) and unsupervised learning (exploring unlabeled data structures) already introduced, semi-supervised learning sits between supervised and unsupervised learning, using a small amount of labeled data and a large amount of unlabeled data to enhance learning, especially for scenarios with insufficient labeled data. It can also be used for classification, regression, and clustering problems [ 106 ]. At present, semi-supervised learning is gradually attracting attention in the materials field. Huo et al. [ 351 ] used semi-supervised learning to classify inorganic material synthesis steps from a natural language text, first clustering keywords in an unsupervised approach and then associating the steps with material synthesis categories guided by a small amount of annotation, ultimately constructing a machine-readable database. Jia et al. [ 352 ] combined an HTC and a semi-supervised strategy of positive-unlabeled learning (PU-learning) to discover potential thermoelectric materials, predicted the probability of unlabeled materials belonging to the positive examples by matching the literature title labeling of the positive example data, and filtered out 40 candidate materials. However, a key challenge of semi-supervised learning is that introducing unlabeled data may lead to performance degradation [ 106 ], which perhaps limits its application to HEA predictions. Further development of semi-supervised learning methods allows a better understanding of the complex structure behind the data and patterns between unlabeled data. These advantages are crucial to overcoming the bottleneck of the insufficient HEA data, especially labeled data, and also contribute to unraveling the complex predictive mechanisms behind the data models and deepening the understanding of HEA’s underlying physics and chemistry mechanisms.

sections.heading: Reinforcement Learning (RL)
paragraphs: Reinforcement learning is an ML field focusing on how an agent can act within an environment to maximize cumulative rewards. Inspired by behaviorist psychology, RL allows agents to learn through environmental interactions rather than explicit instructions or labeled datasets. In an iterative-learning process, the agent adapts its strategy based on its actions’ outcomes (rewards or penalties). Unlike supervised learning, RL does not require pre-defined input/output datasets; instead, it balances exploration (trying new actions) and exploitation (using known effective actions) [ 353 ]. Environments are often modeled as Markov-decision processes (MDPs), enabling dynamic-programming techniques [ 107 ] to solve RL problems. RL has been applied to build adaptive-counseling models using ANNs to learn from human tutors [ 354 ]. Many fundamental RL problems can be modeled as MDPs with stochastic rules [ 340 ]. Currently, RL is being explored as a highly promising ML method for its potential in a closed-loop, intrinsic-alloy compositional design for manual synthesis and characterization. Xian et al. [ 355 ] demonstrated training an RL agent on a dataset with 112 kinds of alloys, improving training efficiency using an acquisition function, such as expected improvement (EI), as a reward. Experimental feedback enabled the agent to progressively explore new and potentially superior compositional regions. The RL method offers instructive and versatile capabilities, while its application in the HEA design is currently constrained by the high cost of traditional experimental feedback. Therefore, developing HTE and characterization techniques within the HEA field promises a bright future for the RL-guided HEA design.

To provide a concise overview, Table  1  summarizes the different categories of ML algorithms, including advantages, disadvantages, and typical applications of ML algorithms in the context of HEA research. This table aids readers in navigating the landscape of ML for HEA research, facilitating the selection of the most appropriate algorithm for a given task based on data availability and desired outcomes.

sections.heading: Applications and Strategies for HEA Design
Predictive Modeling for HEA Properties
paragraphs: ML has been extensively employed to aid the HEA design, particularly for predicting phase selections and mechanical properties, such as YS, UTS, hardness, wear resistance, and fatigue. “ ML Algorithms for Assisted HEA Design ” has detailed various ML models for predicting these properties, and numerous reviews have summarized the ML-assisted prediction of HEA phase selection, mechanical, and magnetic properties, or multi-objective optimization. In addition, the process design associated with HEA fabrication processes, such as additive manufacturing, has also been considered using the ML-assisted design [ 90 ,  92 ,  93 ,  95 ,  341 ,  356 ,  357 ,  358 – 359 ]. Recently, ML applications to predict the oxidation and corrosion resistance behavior of HEAs have also been gaining attention [ 100 ]. This section will further explore the challenges of predicting HEA’s oxidation and corrosion resistance behavior. The attention will be on ML methods to assist in deepening the understanding of the complex correlation between the oxidation and corrosion mechanisms of HEAs and their components, as well as to accelerate the rapid screening of new compositions of HEA with oxidant or corrosion resistance.

sections.heading: Oxidation Resistance
paragraphs: Due to their excellent YS at ambient and elevated temperatures, HEAs are potential candidates for high-temperature structural applications, such as aero-engines, nuclear reactors, and thermal-protection systems [ 360 ]. Future technologies will require increasingly high operating temperatures, making it necessary to develop alloys operating under extreme conditions [ 361 ]. Oxidation resistance is a crucial performance metric for HEAs in long-term, high-temperature service, as oxidation significantly degrades mechanical properties [ 362 ]. Numerous experimental studies have investigated the oxidation behavior of HEAs [ 17 ,  363 ,  364 ,  365 ,  366 ,  367 – 368 ], providing valuable data for ML-assisted prediction of antioxidant properties. However, the oxidation behavior of HEAs is complex and is not only related to the interaction tendencies of the compositional elements and the environment [ 369 ] but is also significantly influenced by the chemical composition and structural-evolution mechanisms of the oxide scales [ 370 ]. The predictive capability of any ML model relies on training data that accurately correlates alloy compositions, environmental conditions, and oxidation resistance indices [ 361 ]. Therefore, selecting appropriate descriptors and constructing reliable databases and ML models to create a virtual sample space is essential for ML-based screening of HEA compositions with enhanced oxidation resistance.

Gorsse et al. [ 361 ] constructed XGBoost and GBDT models to predict the mass gain of oxidized HEA samples. They used 886 observations from the literature, incorporating alloy composition, oxidation temperature, and exposure time as input parameters. To explore compositional relationships, they employed a compositional similarity network (Fig.  12 a), where nodes represent compositions and closer clustering indicates higher similarity. Three prominent regions (orange, violet, and blue) represent areas where Cr, Nb, and Al often dominate. Noting the low node density in the central region, suggesting incomplete compositional exploration, they synthesized and incorporated data from nine randomly selected alloys. Figure  12 b presents the GBDT model’s accuracy in predicting specific mass gain after 3 to 100 h of oxidation in air at 600–1400 °C. The black dots on the red edges represent MAEs for an unseen test set of five alloys. The authors also suggested exploring the Pilling-Bedworth ratio to assess volumetric changes during oxidation relative to the original HEA, as mass gain alone may not fully capture oxidation resistance. Dong et al. [ 371 ] used an ML-integrated workflow to guide the design of FeCrAlNiCu-based HEAs. Their dataset comprised 482 literature entries, including chemical composition, exposure temperature, exposure time, and weight gain. They evaluated various ML models (including DT, RF, XGBoost, Adaboost, GDBT, and KNN), ultimately selecting the most reliable RF model to predict HEA weight gain. Experimental validation at 1,100 °C on AlCrCuFeNi alloys confirmed the potential of ML as an effective tool for designing HEAs with excellent oxidation resistance. They visualized the effect of compositional variations on oxidation resistance (Fig.  12 c), plotting the predicted weight gain of 3003 kinds of virtual HEA samples after 100 h of exposure to 1100 °C air. Figure  12 d statistically shows the elemental occurrence frequency in HEAs classified by weight gain, revealing that Ni, Cu, Co, Mo, and Si may contribute to improved high-temperature oxidation resistance. Wei et al. [ 372 ] explored incorporating the correlation between the FeCrAlCoNi-based HEA oxidation weight gain and test conditions into the Arrhenius equation. Their dataset included alloy composition, experimental temperature, exposure time, and oxidation weight gain. Feature importance was analyzed using XGBoost, while a tree-based classification method [tree classifier for linear regression (TCLR)] extracted the time index and activation energy. The predicted ranges of activation energy ( Q ) and time index ( m ) showed good agreement with experimental results. Based on the prediction process (Fig.  12 e), they derived highly explanatory formulae describing elevated-temperature HEA oxidation behavior. ML has excellent potential for predicting the antioxidant properties of HEAs and elucidating their oxidation mechanism. Future studies could consider incorporating more complex descriptors (e.g., oxidative scale-related features) and combining physical or chemical formulations (e.g., oxidation-kinetic models) with ML models. These strategies will contribute to rapidly screening and developing HEAs with superior antioxidant properties. Fig. 12 a  Alloy-composition-similarity network. It visualizes the relationships between the different alloy compositions in the database, each represented by a node color-coded by the dominant element in the molar percentage. Connections between nodes are colored according to the primary component of their average composition, and this similarity measures how closely the alloys fit together in the hyperdimensional composition space. The central region with fewer nodes highlights the less explored compositional areas and complements the data with nine randomly sampled and tested alloys in this region.  b  The accuracy of the GBDT model in predicting specific mass increments after oxidation in air at 600–1400 °C for 3 to 100 h. The black dots on the red edges indicate the MAEs for the unseen test set of the five attendant alloys [ 361 ].  c  The weight gain of 3003 kinds of virtual HEA samples was predicted by the ML for 100 h of exposure in the air at 1100 °C.  d  The statistical number of occurrences of elements in HEAs was classified according to their weight gain for 100 h of exposure at 1100 °C in the air [ 371 ].  e  Schematic workflow of a domain knowledge-guided ML. It shows the collection of high-temperature oxidation data from the literature, the analysis of the diversity of the raw data, the  Q  and  m  extracted by TCLR, the physical extracted values constructed as a function of composition, and the prediction of the final analytical formulae [ 372 ]

sections.heading: Corrosion Resistance
paragraphs: Corrosion can seriously affect the life and safety of engineering materials, which is a key issue in the automotive, marine, aerospace, energy, and biomedical fields [ 373 ]. The need to develop high-performance corrosion-resistant materials is becoming more and more urgent. However, relatively little research has been conducted on the corrosion resistance of HEAs [ 14 ,  15 ,  24 ,  25 ,  374 ,  375 ,  376 – 377 ], which has resulted in insufficient data to support the application of traditional methods, such as DFT, MD, and thermodynamic simulations [ 378 ]. The main challenge in the ML-assisted prediction of HEAs’ corrosion resistance is the complexity of the corrosion process. Corrosion performance is influenced by various factors, including environmental conditions, chemical compositions, and microstructures. In addition, understanding the corrosion mechanism and different corrosion types adds to the difficulty of material design [ 88 ]. Several studies have been conducted on constructing reliable corrosion databases and identifying valid corrosion descriptors [ 379 ,  380 – 381 ]. Commonly used descriptors for corrosion resistance predictions include three key descriptors for predicting corrosion rates: medium pH, halide concentration, and elemental composition with the lowest reduction potential [ 382 ]. Cohesion energy, oxide-formation energy, and surface enrichment of passivating elements linked to surface passivation, dissolution, and microstructure-related corrosion resistance are also considered as valuable descriptors [ 383 ]. The current research on the ML-assisted prediction of the HEA corrosion resistance still focuses on screening suitable descriptors and constructing suitable datasets.

The ML-assisted prediction of the corrosion-resistant behavior of HEAs has made initial progress. Ozdemir et al. [ 384 ] constructed a dataset comprising the alloy composition, corrosion potential ( E corr ), polarization experimental temperature, electrolyte type, and pH, using data gleaned from the literature. Employing an RF model, they predicted the  E corr  of HEAs within the HfNbTaTiZr alloy system for biomedical applications, achieving a high  R 2  value of 0.98. Experimental validation of the predictions demonstrated the potential of ML for corrosion studies, even with limited datasets. Zou et al. [ 378 ] compiled a dataset of 430 data points from the literature, encompassing alloy composition and state, preparation method, solution environment, test temperature, reference electrode,  E corr , and corrosion current density ( i corr ). XGBoost and GBDT models achieved high  R 2  values (0.8102 and 0.8464), demonstrating a good generalization ability. By constructing a physics-based ML framework, Zeng et al. [ 88 ] focused on augmenting data-driven methods with physical insights, particularly in scenarios with limited descriptors. They predicted single-phase formability using RF modeling, Pilling–Bedworth ratios of passivating elements via high-fidelity ML interatomic potentials, surface energy, and a combination of these three-corrosion metrics (believed to influence pitting corrosion) to predict the relationship between the chemical composition and corrosion resistance in HEAs for the first time. This approach was experimentally validated on HEAs within the AlCrFeCoNi system.

Researchers are also exploring NLP and HTE design methods to expand the data sources for predicting the corrosion resistance behavior of HEAs. Sasidhar et al. [ 190 ] proposed a strategy combining NLP and DNNs to predict the corrosion resistance of HEAs. Figure  13 a details the NLP pipeline: the text is first tokenized, then converted into vectors (word embeddings), and finally, key information is extracted using a recurrent-neural network (RNN). The RNN’s ability to handle out-of-vocabulary words encountered during model application but not in the training data is a key advantage. They then integrated the NLP-processed textual data with digital features and used the DNN model to predict the pitting potential. Figure  13 b illustrates the text-incorporated model’s application in optimizing alloy compositions for enhanced corrosion resistance. It presents the compositional evolution of a NiFeCrCo HEA during the optimization process, aiming to maximize pitting potential. The results demonstrate that the text-incorporated model, unlike the simple DNN model lacking textual input, predicts a significant contribution of molybdenum and copper to the improved pitting resistance of the NiFeCrCo HEA. Furthermore, it highlights the critical role of interstitial N and C elements in the pitting resistance of the NiFeCrCo HEA. This text-incorporated model can integrate processing history and electrochemical test methods to more accurately identify the contribution of different alloying elements toward pitting resistance in specific electrochemical environments. Goh et al. [ 385 ] generated the first large-scale, standardized molten salt corrosion dataset using an HTE approach (Fig.  13 c). Alloys were fabricated via additive manufacturing and in situ alloying within the CrFeMnNi compositional space and subjected to standardized corrosion tests. Analysis of SHAP values (Fig.  13 d) revealed that the bulk diffusion coefficient of the noble element Ni was the most significant (in comparison with the reactive elements Mn, Cr, and Fe) and consistent predictor of corrosion resistance in CrFeMnNi alloys. Low Ni diffusion exhibited a weak inhibitory effect on corrosion, whereas high Ni diffusion exacerbated it. This observation is supported by the scanning electron microscope (SEM) observations: low Ni diffusion regions (left) displayed intergranular corrosion, while high Ni diffusion regions (right) exhibited surface roughening and dealloying of the ligament structure, as shown in Fig.  12 d. This finding offers new avenues for designing corrosion-resistant alloys. Combining human intuition with the strengths of ML will accelerate our fundamental understanding of corrosion mechanisms in HEAs. Although research on the ML-assisted prediction of HEA corrosion resistance continues to be explored, it is constrained by the complexity of the corrosion mechanisms and the availability of data. These studies demonstrate the efficacy of ML as a powerful tool for developing HEAs with enhanced corrosion resistance. Fig. 13 a  The NLP process consists of three steps: text tokenization, word-embedding vector transformation, and extracting key information using RNNs.  b  The evolution of the composition of the NiFeCrCo HEA during the optimization process. The process-aware model can predict the significant role of molybdenum and copper elements, as well as interstitial nitrogen and carbon elements, in improving the pitting resistance of the alloy compared to a simplified DNN model without textual information [ 190 ].  c  Schematic of the HTE methodology for processing, corrosion testing, and characterization of CrFeMnNi HEAs.  d  Comparisons of the corrosion profiles of the high Ni diffusion alloys with the low Ni diffusion alloys, showing that the high Ni diffusion alloys exhibited a higher overall degree of corrosion. The kinetic behavior of the element, Ni, is the primary driver for the corrosion of the selected alloys in molten halides [ 385 ]

sections.heading: Advanced ML Strategies for HEA Design
Active-Learning (AL) Strategy
paragraphs: The active-learning (AL) strategy efficiently explores the vast material-design space, iteratively selecting the most informative data points to rapidly optimize target performance and accelerate the discovery of new materials. Benefits include reduced required training data, accelerated model training, shorter training time, and high classification accuracy with minimal labeled samples [ 386 ]. As a subfield of ML, AL has emerged as an alternative to material discovery [ 387 ]. It uses an agent model to iteratively select the most informative unseen data points to improve the model’s predictive power [ 388 ]. The previous model guides the next set of experiments, and the newly generated data are used to update the model iteratively. AL is expected to reduce the computational cost of alloy design and integrate and guide experimental data and processes [ 389 ].

AL strategies effectively address the “small-sample” problem often encountered in HEA predictions. Several studies [ 79 ,  386 ,  389 ,  390 ,  391 – 392 ] have employed AL to aid the HEA design. Li et al. [ 390 ] utilized an AL loop with VEC constraints (Fig.  14 a) to train an agent model using a small dataset of only 50 alloys (features included elemental compositions, tensile strengths, and elongations). By leveraging the domain knowledge regarding the strength-ductility trade-off and considering VECs influencing the hard BCC and soft FCC phase fractions, they reduced the search space from approximately 421,000 to 328,000 compositions. Their recommended strategy for the experimental alloy selection includes the exploration (maximum uncertainty), exploitation (maximum mean), and a strategy to balance both exploration and exploitation using Bayesian optimization [ 393 ]. Through six AL iterations, 18 kinds of alloys were prepared and characterized. As shown in Fig.  14 b, the cast alloy Al 19 Co 2 Cr 18 Fe 21 Ni 40  ultimately achieved a UTS of 1258 MPa and 17.3% elongation. The mechanical properties of the newly synthesized alloys were comparable to those within the training data and even rivaled some thermo-mechanically treated alloys. The clustering of data points around the diagonal further validates the robustness of the ML model. Sulley et al. [ 391 ] employed an AL approach based on Bayesian optimization and neural networks to efficiently explore the vast compositional space of HEAs, focusing on stable phase predictions (Fig.  14 c). Figure  14 d illustrates the application of this framework using the CoCrNi-ternary system. Model uncertainties were typically the highest near phase boundaries, suggesting these regions as optimal sampling locations. By concentrating data collections in the high-uncertainty areas, they achieved 0.95 test accuracy using only 27% of the experimental HEA dataset, comparable to the 0.946 accuracy of an RF model trained on 80% of the entire dataset (2198 quinary HEAs). Similarly, using only about 2% of the CALPHAD dataset, they achieved a phase-prediction accuracy exceeding 0.96, comparable to the > 0.97 accuracy of an XGBoost model trained on a near-complete dataset (664,650 quinary HEAs). The AL strategy is expected to significantly improve the computational efficiency of the HEA-design-space exploration and guide the efficient design of novel HEAs. Fig. 14 a  AL cycle based on VEC constraints for the HEA design, including steps of dataset construction, model training, domain-knowledge application, alloy design, experimental validation, and feedback.  b  Comparison of predicted UTS and measured values for 18 kinds of new synthetic alloys; elongation and VEC distributions for collected and synthetic alloys; comparison of UTS and elongation for collected and synthetic alloys; and engineering tensile curves of the Al 12 Co 2 Cr 18 Fe 21 Ni 40 , Al 18 Co 20 Fe 20 Ni 42  [ 394 ], AlCoCr 1.8 FeNi 2  [ 395 ], and Al 19 Fe 20 Co 20 Ni 41  [ 396 ] HEAs [ 390 ].  c  The general framework of the AL approach.  d  A simple example of the AL framework with a Co–Cr–Ni ternary-alloy system. The model typically exhibits the highest degree of uncertainty near phase boundaries, suggesting it will focus on sampling near these boundaries [ 391 ]

sections.heading: Transfer-Learning (TL) Strategy
paragraphs: Applying ML to the efficient design of high-performance HEAs presents two significant challenges: model generalization and data scarcity [ 397 ]. Conventional ML models often exhibit relatively poor generalization in the extrapolation space (i.e., beyond the training data distribution), even when demonstrating strong performance in CV. This data scarcity further exacerbates the generalization problem. AL offers an iterative approach to discovering high-performance material, but the costs associated with the HEA fabrication and characterization are relatively high, and researchers have reduced the cost of its application by attempting to enhance the generalization capabilities of the model. The applications of the priori physical knowledge to aid traditional-ML models help to improve the extrapolation performance and reduce the data dependence, but the lack of understanding about HEA mechanisms, such as deformation, oxidation, and corrosion, limits the development of features in related areas [ 398 ].

Transfer learning (TL), also known as knowledge transfer, offers a promising solution. Rather than directly training a model with limited target data, TL constructs a robust base model using pre-trained parameters from a large dataset. A smaller target dataset is then fine-tuned for optimal performance [ 399 ]. TL can effectively prevent overfitting, speed up training, and achieve high performance even on small datasets by sharing knowledge among related domain models [ 400 ]. In addition, TL facilitates feature-fusion studies to generate more accurate and diverse feature sets [ 401 ]. These advantages are crucial to achieve the efficient design of HEAs. Studies employing TL for HEA performance predictions typically train models on the extensive glass-forming ability (GFA) for metallic-glass datasets (exceeding 10,000 entries) before fine-tuning them on smaller HEA datasets [ 400 ]. The periodic table representation (PTR) is frequently utilized for automated feature extraction and knowledge transfer. PTR maps material compositions onto a two-dimensional image resembling the periodic table, enabling CNNs to learn correlations among compositions, elemental positions, and material properties [ 402 ].

Feng et al. [ 400 ] posit that while the output domains differ (binary classification for GFA prediction and multi-category classification for HEA phase prediction), the input domains for these two tasks are highly correlated. These alloys share numerous constituent elements; some amorphous alloys are also HEAs, and established ML descriptors for GFA and HEA are often transferable. Consequently, a CNN-based automatic feature extractor that is effective for GFA predictions should also prove applicable to HEA predictions. Based on this premise, they developed a high-performance model using a limited dataset capable of simultaneously distinguishing five distinct phases within HEAs. The workflow of their proposed generative-transfer-deep-learning (GTDL) framework (green-solid arrows) and traditional ML (black-dashed arrows) is shown in Fig.  15 a. Traditional methods lack the ability to extract features and knowledge migration automatically. It shows the flow of a dataset assembly, data representation, ML, knowledge migration, an example PTR, and the VGG-like convolutional neural network architecture used. Their GTDL framework was successfully deployed for the HEA development with small datasets. Wang et al. [ 403 ] proposed an elemental-convolutional neural network (ECNet) to leverage the knowledge gained from non-primary element alloys for predicting the performance of HEAs within the FeNiCoCrMn/Pd system, using DFT data and TL. ECNet’s elemental features (as generic descriptors) maintain high accuracy even with small datasets and successfully predict formation energies, magnetic moments, and local displacements in sub-ternary and quintuple element systems, thus deepening the understanding of the physical properties of these HEAs. To systematically compare feature input methods and model selection, Arindam Debnath et al. [ 404 ] analyzed the frequency of elemental occurrences within the GFA, HEA phase, hardness, and yield strength datasets using the PTR method (Fig.  15 b). They compared various structuring schemes (Fig.  15 c), including fully unstructured representations, one-dimensional arrangements, and two-dimensional spatial structuring. Figure  15 d shows with the results of TL on HEA phases that in both the single-task deep-learning and TL scenarios, spatial structuring (arranging elements according to their chemical significance) generally outperforms unstructured and randomly ordered representations. However, single-task RF models using atomic fractions as input features achieved comparable performance. These results suggest that the judicious selection of feature input methods and models is crucial for ensuring the effectiveness and accuracy of TL in the HEA design. Fig. 15 a  The workflows of the proposed GTDL framework (green-solid line) and traditional ML (black-dashed line). Traditional ML lacks the automatic feature extraction and knowledge-transfer capabilities. It illustrates a dataset assembly, data representation, ML, and TL alongside an example of PTR and the architecture of the VGG-like convolutional neural network employed [ 400 ].  b  The frequency of elemental occurrences is shown for both the GFA dataset (left) and the HEA phase dataset (right). The HEA dataset is smaller than the GFA dataset and exhibits a more restricted range of elemental compositions.  c  Various data structuring schemes are presented, including fully unstructured representations (DNN), structured one-dimensional representations (CNN1), and structured two-dimensional representations (CNN2).  d  This panel compares the performance of RF models for the HEA phase prediction using different input features: alloy compositions and TL features extracted from the trained DNNs/CNNs. Generally, spatial-representation schemes outperform unstructured and randomly ordered schemes, which arrange elements according to their chemical significance [ 404 ]

While TL holds broad applicability, its effectiveness depends critically on the correlation between source and target domains [ 405 ]. Significant discrepancies can lead to negative transfer, diminishing the pre-trained model’s performance on the target task [ 406 ]. This risk is particularly prominent in the design of HEAs, where the coupling effect between composition-phase-structure properties is characterized by strong nonlinearities (e.g., the dynamic effect of multi-component SRO on YS). Currently, a variety of strategies can be applied to mitigate this risk of negative transfer: (1) Domain-similarity assessment: Prior to the application of TL, the similarity between source and target domains needs to be systematically assessed, including the consistency of component space, physical mechanisms, and data distribution. This assessment can be done using a variety of dispersion-based-distributional-distance metrics, such as maximum mean discrepancy (MMD) [ 407 ,  408 ], Kullback–Leibler (KL) divergence [ 409 ], Jensen–Shannon (JS) divergence [ 410 ], and Wasserstein distance [ 411 ] to measure the marginal and conditional distributional discrepancies of the domains [ 412 ]. In addition, the Hilbert–Schmidt Independence Criterion (HSIC) [ 413 ] applies to the analysis of kernel spatial dependencies, while correlation coefficients [ 414 ] and mutual information [ 415 ] can assess the statistical dependence between variables [ 412 ] capture linear and nonlinear associations, respectively. For example, fuzzy systems are suitable for handling uncertainty, while instance reweighting is suitable for certain boosting-based methods [ 405 ]. Feng et al. [ 400 ] provide an example of domain similarity analysis, revealing shared chemical elements between metallic-glass and HEA datasets, suggesting feasibility for knowledge transfer. (2) Fine-tuning strategy: Rather than naively accepting all pre-trained weights, the pre-trained model was fine-tuned to adapt it to the target domain. This involved adjusting the learning rate [ 398 ], selectively freezing layers, often retaining pre-trained weights for deeper layers to preserve generalized features learned from the source domain [ 416 ], and progressively unfreezing layers, starting from the output and moving toward the input, and controlling the degree of transfer [ 398 ,  416 ,  417 ]. These strategies preserve generalized features from the source domain while allowing for target-specific refinement. (3) Multi-source transfer and domain adaptation: To leverage more information and minimize negative transfer, explore multi-source TL [ 406 ,  418 ]. Furthermore, domain adaptation techniques like transfer component analysis (TCA) [ 419 ,  420 ] were considered to reduce inter-domain dataset bias and learn domain-invariant features. (4) Additional strategies: Other methods, including instance-based transfer learning (e.g., TrAdaBoost [ 421 ], GapBoost [ 418 ]), regularization (e.g., L2 regularization) [ 422 ], and fuzzy systems [ 423 ,  424 ], can further reduce negative transfer and improve model generalization. Yang et al. [ 398 ] accelerated single-crystal superalloy design by fine-tuning a pre-trained model on a limited creep dataset, incorporating  γ / γ ʹ interface morphology information. A reduced learning rate minimized bias during fine-tuning, focusing on optimizing Mo and Ta concentrations to predict key properties. This approach enabled the prediction of concentration-dependent formation energies, lattice constants, and magnetic moments within the five-element system. The effectiveness of this TL strategy is highlighted by the successful design of a superalloy demonstrating a creep rupture life of 176 h at 1200 °C and 80 MPa. The framework proposed by Sun et al. [ 416 ] generates data containing elemental and structural information for data augmentation and incorporates TL principles. It also offers a promising approach to mitigate negative transfer. Mitigating the risk of negative transfer is crucial for the effective application of TL to HEAs, particularly when dealing with limited datasets. Future research needs to explore the closed-loop integration of TL with HTE further, e.g., an active-TL framework based on Bayesian optimization can dynamically guide the replenishment of critical experimental samples.

sections.heading: Inverse-Design Strategy
paragraphs: Traditional ML approaches to materials design identify target materials by predicting the properties of candidate materials and screening them within the chemical space. This forward approach, while effective, presents two key challenges: efficient exploration of the vast chemical space and rapid, accurate development of materials combining stability with desirable properties [ 425 ,  426 ]. Despite improvements in advanced algorithms, such as AL and TL, it is still not possible to evaluate and screen all possible elemental compositions. More importantly, searches based on known materials can miss out on new materials with better properties [ 427 ]. Inverse design searches for the corresponding structure from the target properties, which provides a novel way to discover new materials [ 428 ]. Rather than conducting a global search across the entire compositional space, it generates new alloys that meet the desired criteria along an optimal path. Currently, inverse design employs two primary strategies: global optimization within the compositional space [ 429 ] and data-driven generative models [ 427 ].

Considering that the forward-design methods are effective, computationally expensive, and time-consuming, the inverse-design methods can struggle to find optimal solutions due to potential discontinuities in the attribute space. Debnath et al. [ 430 ] quantitatively compared two forward-design methods and one inverse-design method for the HEA design (Fig.  16 a). The forward-design approach (blue box), which iteratively refines designs based on the existing knowledge and experimental measurements (“oracle queries”), is slow and costly. The screening or optimization-based forward-design approach (orange box) uses agent models to predict material properties and optimize design variables over multiple iterations. Although more efficient than rational design, it remains constrained by the search space. Conversely, the inverse-design approach (green box) begins with the target performance. It utilizes a DNN-based generative model [e.g., variational autoencoders (VAEs) or conditional generative adversarial networks (cGANs)] to learn the data distribution and generate candidate-alloy compositions that satisfy the target performance, which is then experimentally validated. By comparing the inverse-design approach to the forward search and HT-screening scheme, the researchers found that the inverse-design approach identifies combinations of components with a higher predicted UTS under the same constraints. It is relatively straightforward to consider additional material properties. Wang et al. [ 317 ] employed a conditional random search as an inverse predictor to design HEAs with higher YS or UTS than existing high-performance HEAs, achieving excellent strength and ductility. Raman et al. [ 114 ] constructed a simulated HEA dataset comprising binary to senary systems of nine refractory elements (Cr, Hf, Mo, Nb, Ta, Ti, V, W, and Zr) combined in 1% compositional increments. This dataset trained a cGAN model consisting of four fully connected layers (three hidden and one output) conditioned on seven target attributes: d-electron parameter, price, SS strengthening, mixing entropy (Δ S mix ), fracture toughness, density, and hardness. The model successfully predicted two HEAs with optimal density-strength combinations, and with microstructure predictions consistent with CALPHAD and Scheil simulations. Figure  16 b illustrates the prediction process and the experimental and CALPHAD validation results for the two selected alloys. The present work demonstrates the effectiveness of a data-driven inverse-design approach for identifying promising new HEAs. Li et al. [ 431 ] presented an ML framework integrating the forward and inverse design to predict high-strength and low-density HEAs, as illustrated in Fig.  16 c. Leveraging the JMatPro software [ 432 ] and a nickel-based-superalloy database [ 433 ], they supplemented missing data on grain sizes, particle sizes and volume fractions of  γ ʹ, and lattice misfits. Combined with compositional data, these parameters were used to train a highly accurate ( R 2  > 0.95) model for predicting the YS of HEAs, forming the basis for the subsequent inverse design. This inverse-design process aimed to identify alloy compositions corresponding to target YS values within the vast compositional space. They incorporated two key constraints: alloy densities and a cluster formula representing the atomic structure of HEAs. Integrating these constraints into the inverse-design algorithm efficiently searches for components that minimize the difference between the target and predicted values of YS. This inverse-design approach successfully identified three novel HEAs with target YS values of 1050, 1150, and 1350 MPa, respectively. The expected strengths of these alloys (1057, 1151, and 1346 MPa, respectively) with excellent high-temperature properties and creep resistance were experimentally verified, and their deformation mechanisms were investigated. Augmenting the inverse-design strategy with the domain-specific knowledge and forward-design models offers a reliable and valuable method for realizing high-performance HEAs through the automated-ML exploration of the extensive compositional space. Although currently limited by data availability and algorithm complexity, its potential to predict novel compositions within unexplored compositional spaces and its high efficiency are promising for future HEA development. Fig. 16 a  A rational forward-design method (blue box) based on existing knowledge and experimental measurements (Oracle queries). A screening or optimization forward-design approach (orange box) that uses an agent model to predict material properties and optimize design variables through multiple iterations. A generative-inverse model (green box) learns the data distribution from the target performance using a DNN-based generative model to discover materials that satisfy the target performance [ 430 ].  b  The basic flow of the inverse-design process is based on the cGANs model, validation results from experiments, and CLAPHAD calculations for two alloys screened with an optimal density-strength combination [ 114 ].  c  A schematic workflow for designing low-density and high-strength HEAs using the ML. Before the ML implementation, the sample data in the database were preprocessed by the JMatPro software based on the specialized-domain knowledge. Subsequently, the forward design was used to train models and establish relationships between the input components, microstructural features, and output YS values. In the inverse design, constraints based on the cluster formulation and densities were incorporated to refine the search for suitable components [ 431 ]

sections.heading: Quantum-Machine-Learning (QML) Strategy
paragraphs: Given the immense potential of TM and NLP to enhance the “4 Vs” of data science [ 191 ] in the field of HEAs (as discussed in section “ Literature and Experimental Data ”), the volume of HEA data is expected to grow exponentially, underscoring the need for innovative ML methods. Quantum computing [ 434 ] is an emerging computational paradigm based on quantum mechanics that offers a fundamentally different approach to information processing. By exploiting phenomena, such as superposition and entanglement, quantum computers use the behavior of subatomic particles such as photons and electrons to perform calculations and process information [ 435 ]. Compared to classical supercomputers, quantum computers operate at dramatically higher speeds. For example, a team led by Google used a 54-quantum-bit processor to complete a task in about 200 s, whereas a conventional supercomputer would have taken an estimated 10,000 years to accomplish the task [ 436 ]. The potential benefits of quantum computing make it possible to outperform classical-computational methods in the large-scale information processing [ 437 ], providing possible solutions to the challenges posed by the exponential growth in data volumes.

The applications of the quantum computing in ML, known as QML, are already being explored [ 438 ,  439 – 440 ]. The QML strategy seeks to design and implement quantum software to accelerate ML tasks [ 435 ]. Most state-of-the-art classical-ML algorithms have quantum counterparts [ 437 ], such as the quantum SVM [ 441 ] and the quantum GAN [ 442 ,  443 ]. There are two main approaches to the QML [ 444 ]: pure-quantum algorithms (e.g., quantum-Fourier transforms [ 445 ] and quantum-phase estimation [ 446 ]), which require fault-tolerant quantum computers and are not yet available. The second approach uses hybrid-quantum-classical algorithms (e.g., variational-quantum eigensolver [ 447 ,  448 ], quantum-approximate-optimization algorithm [ 449 ], and quantum-circuit learning [ 450 ]), which operate parameterization on the noisy-intermediate-scale quantum (NISQ) [ 451 ] device to quantum circuits and classical computations [ 452 ] to solve variational-optimization problems. The applications of the QML strategy in the field of HEA are receiving increasing attention. Brown et al. [ 444 ] investigated hybrid-quantum–classical ANN models for predicting HEA phases based on chemical compositions. Using a subset of the Miracle and Senkov datasets [ 47 ], they represented HEA compositions with elemental-molar ratios and ket vectors (Dirac notation) as inputs, with the corresponding phases as outputs. The quantum simulator and hardware were employed in the hybrid-quantum–classical-ML computations to predict SS, IM, and mixed (SS + IM) phases. Results from quantum simulators closely matched those of classical ANNs, while quantum-hardware implementations exhibited slightly lower accuracy due to the limitations of NISQ devices. This work serves as a proof-of-concept for quantum-enhanced-HEA design and proposes an alternative-data-encoding scheme for future research. QML holds significant promise for advancing ML, but its full realization depends on future developments in quantum hardware to address current limitations in qubit quality, speed, and scale [ 436 ,  453 ]. The convergence of quantum computing and ML represents a promising frontier for the future of intelligent data processing.

sections.heading: Model Interpretation and Analysis
paragraphs: ML, particularly deep learning, has made remarkable strides in recent years, but its powerful predictive capabilities often come at the expense of interpretability. A trade-off frequently exists between model accuracy and explainability [ 454 ,  455 ]. The “black-box” nature of DNN models, in particular, hinders understanding of their decision-making processes. As these models become more widely used, it is critical to explain their decision-making processes. Explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) aims to increase model transparency and explainability, enhance trust, help detect bias, improve performance, and extract knowledge. XAI’s explanatory methods can be categorized as post-hoc or ante-hoc: post-hoc explanations utilize external data or agent models to explain decisions from a practical-application standpoint, while ante-hoc explanations focus on the overall logic of the model’s operation from a theoretical perspective. Ante-hoc interpretability is inherent to the model, whereas post-hoc interpretability relies on external tools. Most common interpretation techniques, such as saliency maps and feature-importance analysis, fall under the post-hoc category. Both ante-hoc and post-hoc interpretations can be implemented at global or local levels: global interpretations target the entire model and input space, while local interpretations focus on specific parts of the model (e.g., functional forms, parameters, and computations) or input space (e.g., specific data instances) [ 456 ].

Currently, the interpretation methods used for ML-assisted HEA predictions are usually post-hoc and mainly include SHAP, partial dependence plot (PDP) [ 457 ], individual conditional expectation (ICE), centered ICE (cICE) [ 458 ], accumulated local effect (ALE) [ 459 ], and local interpretable model-agnostic explanation (LIME) [ 460 ] methods. Friedman’s PDP method shows the average effect of individual features on the predicted outcome. ICE and cICE further reveal heterogeneity due to feature interactions. The PDP plots the mean-effect curve, and the ICE plots a curve for each sample, thus revealing individual differences. The average of the ICE curves is the PDP curve for the predictor of interest. However, the correlation of characteristics affects both PDP and ICE [ 461 ]. ALE solves the possible false assumptions about highly correlated features by segmenting the calculation [ 462 ]. LIME is capable of interpreting individual predictions of any “black-box” classification model. It provides local explanations by constructing a simple interpretable model near the target prediction, identifying a few key features that impact the classification results of a particular instance [ 463 ]. These methods, especially the SHAP method, have successfully explained the influence of descriptors, such as elemental composition on various aspects, including phases, mechanical, and functional properties [ 80 ,  115 ,  223 ,  264 ,  361 ,  464 ]. The case studies in the preceding chapters have mentioned the SHAP method’s applications. Song et al. [ 465 ] investigated the key features affecting the corrosion resistance of HEAs using interpretable methods, such as SHAP, PDP/ICE, and ALE, as shown in Fig.  17 a–c, respectively. They found that passivating elements, such as Cr and Mo, are essential for increasing the pitting potential with a significant threshold effect, while increasing the Al content increases the pitting size. SHAP values quantified the contribution of individual features to specific predictions, while PDP/ICE plots and ALE provided a more holistic, quantitative interpretation of feature effects. However, all methods can be susceptible to bias when handling anomalous samples, with ALE exhibiting greater sensitivity to outliers than PDP/ICE. Swateelagna et al. [ 466 ] pioneered using LIME to elucidate the predictions of an RF algorithm applied to phase predictions in four novel RHEAs, as illustrated in Fig.  17 d. Blue and orange represent the BCC and SS + IM phases, respectively. The prediction accuracies were 0.75, 0.82, 0.82, and 0.70 for each alloy. The results show that the enthalpy of mixing (Δ H mix ) is critical for phase classification and that the effect of different material descriptors varies for various alloy systems. The application of LIME enhances the understanding of RF predictions and helps to identify critical parameters.
