The widespread use of post-hoc interpretation methods has helped guide the design of novel HEAs, optimize model structures, and improve prediction accuracy. However, few ML-assisted HEA prediction models currently use ante-hoc interpretation methods. This trend may be because of the increased complexity of ante-hoc interpretation methods, while post-hoc interpretation methods are less computationally expensive and easier to understand. For a deeper understanding of “black-box” models, such as DNNs, exploring the application of ante-hoc interpretation methods in HEA prediction models would help gain a deeper understanding of the decision-making mechanisms of the models, which may unlock greater research potential and value. Future research could combine post-hoc interpretation methods with the HEA-domain knowledge and develop ante-hoc interpretation methods to formulate more descriptive and predictive models.

sections.heading: Prospect
paragraphs: With HEA research’s deepening and application areas’ expansion, advanced tools such as HTC, HTE, and ML are becoming increasingly crucial for HEA discovery and mechanistic understanding. However, the application of ML in HEAs still faces many challenges and requires systematic breakthroughs in data scarcity, multi-scale modeling, model performance and interpretability, and efficient experimental validation. In this section, combined with the progress of cutting-edge research and bottlenecks in the field, the following future directions are proposed.

sections.heading: Enrich and Improve Data Resources
paragraphs: High-quality data are the cornerstone of materials innovation. HEAs require comprehensive, reliable, and dynamic databases to drive data-driven discovery. Two priorities emerge to obtain higher-quality datasets: (1) bridging multi-scale data gaps and (2) acquiring data efficiently and deploying intelligent augmentation to overcome experimental bottlenecks.

sections.heading: Multi-scale Data Integration
paragraphs: Effective integration of atomic-scale, mesoscopic, and macroscopic data remains a great challenge at present, as they have different representations, resolutions, and physical meanings. In addition, imbalanced data volumes across scales can introduce modeling biases. Addressing these challenges requires innovative data representation methods that map multi-scale data into a unified feature space, facilitating the construction of comprehensive materials databases. GNNs offer a promising avenue for such integration. By representing atomic structures as graphs, GNNs can learn interatomic interactions and subsequently predict macroscopic properties. Furthermore, GNNs can bridge thermodynamic databases (e.g., CALPHAD) with atomistic simulations, potentially predicting complex phase diagrams. Li et al. [ 467 ] demonstrated this approach by predicting martensitic start temperatures using a GNN informed by a thermodynamically-derived graph, effectively fusing atomic-level thermodynamic parameters with mesoscopic/macroscopic features like composition and grain size. Their work also highlights the ability of graph-based approaches to handle missing data dimensions, a common issue in multi-scale modeling. Another example of multi-scale integration is the work of Altarabsheh et al. [ 468 ]. They combined MD simulations, shape-nucleation theory, nudged elastic band (NEB) methods, and ML models to integrate atomic-scale-interfacial parameters into a continuous medium-scale crystal plasticity finite element analysis (CPFEA) model. This multi-scale approach can simulate the mechanical behavior of materials at larger scales while maintaining atomic-scale accuracy at the interface, resulting in more accurate predictions of the mechanical response of materials. In addition, TM techniques can be utilized to extract information on the composition, properties, and preparation processes of HEA from the literature, which can be supplemented to the database and used to train ML models. The application of TM techniques can extend the data sources and help to discover new relationships between HEA components and properties [ 469 ].

sections.heading: Efficient Data Acquisition and Intelligent Data Enhancement
paragraphs: Acquiring high-quality experimental or simulation data in a limited period is challenging due to the inherent high costs and lengthy timescales associated with experimentation or simulation for HEAs [ 470 ]. Generating physically accurate virtual data for HEAs also presents a significant challenge. Traditional methods of data enhancement can disrupt the fundamental physical properties of materials, limiting their use in this area. Automated experimental platforms and HTC technology provide a way to accelerate data acquisition. Furthermore, combining HTC with ML to construct hybrid models to generate high-fidelity-thermodynamic data is valuable for subsequent data enhancement [ 385 ]. Emerging generative models, such as diffusion models [ 471 ], offer the potential to create high-quality, diverse HEA datasets, effectively mitigating data sparsity. Physics-based data augmentation provides another compelling strategy. By introducing the laws of physics as a priori knowledge, virtual data with both diversity and physical consistency can be synthesized. For instance, combining GANs with physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) [ 472 ] allows the creation of virtual HEA data consistent with thermodynamic principles. Narang et al. [ 473 ] showcase a similar approach, developing an explainable autoencoder PINN (XA-PINN) for the analysis of electromagnetic materials. Their model integrates the Riccati equation [ 474 ], a physics-based constraint, within a neural network and utilizes an autoencoder with GAN (AGAN) for synthetic data generation. This physics-informed strategy generates physically consistent data, addresses data scarcity, and improves model accuracy and generalizability.

sections.heading: Novel-Descriptor Design and Efficient-Descriptor Selection
paragraphs: The multi-component complexity and cross-scale effects of HEAs make the traditional descriptors face bottlenecks. The existing descriptors are difficult to quantitatively characterize the key-microscopic features; moreover, the proliferation in the number of descriptors triggers the dimensionality catastrophe, resulting in overfitting and dramatic increases in computational costs. In view of the above challenges, this section explains the breakthrough paths of ML for the rational design of HEA from the aspects of new-descriptor construction and intelligent-selection methods.

sections.heading: Designing Novel Descriptors for HEAs
paragraphs: To predict the various properties of HEAs more comprehensively, novel descriptors capable of capturing more complex physical and chemical phenomena, such as those describing interatomic interactions and microstructural evolution, need to be designed and improved. In addition to the existing Hume-Rothery rules, descriptors designed at the atomic scale that reflect the physical properties of HEAs and descriptors that address currently poorly understood properties of HEAs (e.g., oxidation and corrosion resistance) could be explored. Furthermore, the influence of SRO on material properties has garnered increasing attention in HEAs [ 475 ]. However, constructing effective SRO descriptors remains a significant challenge due to their localized and non-periodic nature. Vazquez et al. [ 476 ] offered a novel approach to constructing effective SRO descriptors by leveraging a GNN model (M3GNet) in conjunction with DFT to accelerate high-throughput-cluster-expansion calculations and efficiently study chemical ordering, paving the way for the development of more effective SRO descriptors. Departing from manually designed features and physically based descriptors, self-supervised learning has emerged as a powerful method for feature extraction. Wang et al. [ 477 ] demonstrated this with their self-supervised probabilistic model (SSPM) for shape memory alloys. Using a GNN method and a masking strategy, SSPM learns powerful atomic representations from unlabeled crystal structures, outperforming manual-feature design and other descriptors in downstream tasks.

sections.heading: Efficient-Descriptor Selection
paragraphs: Efficient-descriptor selection requires balancing complexity with generalizability to avoid overfitting. Developing effective descriptors is only half the battle; efficiently selecting the most relevant descriptors from a large pool of candidates is equally crucial. Traditional-descriptor-selection methods usually rely on manual experience or simple-statistical analysis. To improve the efficiency of feature selection and optimization, researchers have developed various optimization algorithms, simulated-annealing (SA) algorithms [ 478 ] inspired by the metal-annealing process or GA methods [ 248 ] simulating the natural-selection process. These algorithms can be used to optimize descriptor selections by finding the global optimal solution to find out the most relevant descriptors for the target performance, thus improving the accuracy of ML-assisted HEA predictions. In addition, the automated-machine-learning (AutoML) techniques [ 479 ] (e.g., AutoGluon [ 480 ]) are also receiving widespread attention as an automated approach that can provide efficient, fully automated solutions for feature engineering, model selection, and hyperparameter optimization [ 431 ]. Gao et al. [ 481 ] also used AutoGluon to automatically select the best feature set for predicting the maximal casting diameter of a Fe-based amorphous alloy, ultimately designing a new alloy with excellent properties. These examples highlight the power of AutoML, particularly its ability to streamline feature engineering, minimize human intervention, and democratize access to sophisticated ML tools for accelerated HEAs development.

sections.heading: Application of Machine Learning Interatomic Potential (MLIAP) to Multi-scale Modeling
paragraphs: Accurately predicting the properties of HEAs necessitates bridging various length scales, from the atomic interactions that govern bonding to the microstructural features that influence macroscopic behaviors. This multi-scale challenge is further complicated by the inherent chemical complexity of HEAs, which arises from their multi-component nature and the diverse bonding environments involved. Traditional methods, such as DFT, while precise at the atomic level, are often computationally prohibitive for large-scale simulations. Classical MD can handle larger scales, but its reliance on interatomic potentials often oversimplifies the crucial multi-component interactions in HEAs [ 482 ]. Machine learning interatomic potentials (MLIAPs) [ 483 ,  484 ] offer a solution combining DFT-level accuracy with the efficiency of classical MD. Trained in DFT data, MLIAPs accurately represent the complex atomic interactions in HEAs, capturing diverse chemical environments and multi-component effects. This enables more reliable and extensive MD simulations to investigate dynamic processes, defect behavior, and mechanical properties. The ability of MLIAPs to handle both crystalline and amorphous structures and to bridge disparate lengths and time scales is essential for predicting key HEA properties like SRO, SFEs, and diffusion and for studying defects like grain boundaries and interfaces [ 482 ].

MLIAPs are crucial for multi-scale modeling of HEAs. These potentials, including Gaussian approximation potentials (GAPs) [ 485 ], moment tensor potentials (MTPs) [ 486 ], and neural network potentials (NNPs) [ 487 ], have been successfully applied to model temperature-dependent properties of multi-element alloys [ 488 ] and oxides [ 489 ,  490 – 491 ]. For example, Zheng et al. [ 488 ] used an MTP for the Mo–Ta–Nb–Ti system to investigate the influence of SRO on dislocation glide in MoNbTi and TaNbTi alloys, effectively linking atomic-scale phenomena to mesoscale mechanical behavior. This work highlights the potential of MLIAPs to provide insights into the complex deformation mechanisms in HEAs. The ability of MLIAPs to accurately describe diffusion, particularly in amorphous structures, is demonstrated by Sundar et al. [ 489 ]. In their study of proton diffusion in Al 2 O 3 , they used AL-GAPs, which can be further leveraged to investigate grain boundary diffusion in HEAs, a critical factor influencing their high-temperature performance. Sivaraman et al. [ 490 ] developed accurate HfO 2  potentials using a closed-loop AL scheme guided by experimental data, providing a promising pathway for efficiently generating potential for complex HEAs. This approach is particularly valuable given the vast compositional space and diverse bonding environments present in HEAs. Furthermore, Li et al. [ 491 ] also demonstrated using the deep potential for molecular dynamics (DeePMD) [ 492 ,  493 ] method to simulate chemical reactions and defect evolution, specifically in SiO 2 , which opens exciting possibilities for studying oxidation and corrosion behavior in HEAs. These studies underscore the versatility and power of MLIAPs in addressing critical challenges in HEA research. The ongoing development of MLIAPs and their integration into multi-scale frameworks is crucial for expediting the discovery and design of innovative HEAs.

sections.heading: Explore More Complicated ML Models
paragraphs: Developing HEA with customized features requires advanced ML models that can navigate the vast-component space and complex multi-component interactions. Given that HEA datasets are often limited and potentially unbalanced, these models need to be highly data efficient. In addition, HEA design typically involves optimizing multiple, often competing properties (e.g., strength, ductility, corrosion resistance). Therefore, it is critical to effectively address this multi-objective optimization challenge. In addition, conventional statistical-based ML models find it difficult to capture the physical mechanisms behind the data and how to integrate existing metallurgical knowledge, including phase diagrams, reinforcement mechanisms, and rules of thumb, into the models to improve their predictive accuracy and physical interpretability needs to be further explored.

The TL strategy effectively leverages existing data from related domains, significantly reducing the need for extensive experimental datasets in HEA development. Few-shot meta-transfer learning (FMTL) enhances model performance with limited data by utilizing existing knowledge. [ 494 ]. Integrating QML with language models represents a potentially transformative direction. This synergistic approach can capture complex nonlinear relationships and extract valuable material knowledge from textual data [ 495 ]. As quantum computing hardware matures, this integrated approach holds immense potential for revolutionizing HEA design. It is also crucial to explore multi-objective AL strategies, as these approaches effectively navigate the Pareto frontier while balancing competing objectives [ 392 ,  496 ]. Future work will focus on developing more sophisticated acquisition functions and incorporating uncertainty quantification to further improve the effectiveness of AL in multi-objective HEA design. Focusing on these promising directions will pave the way for more efficient and effective design of HEAs with desired properties.

sections.heading: Enhance Interpretability and Quantify Uncertainty
paragraphs: While recent advances in ML have incredibly advanced materials science, their predictive power often comes at the cost of interpretability. Several key challenges need to be addressed to unlock the full potential of ML in this area. Current XAI methods, such as significance mapping and feature-importance analysis (discussed in section “ Model Interpretation and Analysis ”), primarily provide post-hoc explanations and often struggle to reveal deeper causal relationships in HEA data. In addition, because most existing XAI techniques focus on unimodal data (e.g., compositional or structural parameters), effectively integrating and interpreting information from multimodal (e.g., compositional-microscopic image-spectral couplings) HEA data remains an open question.

Given these challenges, integrating domain knowledge, physical mechanisms, and uncertainty quantification into future research becomes crucial for achieving significant progress. Combining the materials–science-domain knowledge to develop domain-specific XAI techniques, such as attention mechanisms [ 497 ], can help identify microstructural features that play a key role in performance, revealing complex interactions among compositions, structures, and performance. This requires further exploration into effectively incorporating diverse domain knowledge (e.g., phase diagrams, reinforcement mechanisms, empirical rules) into XAI models. Developing more expressive feature representations and XAI techniques capable of handling multimodal data is also crucial. Linking model predictions to known physical mechanisms of HEAs can improve the understanding of model predictions and assist in interpreting complex behaviors, such as oxidation resistance, corrosion resistance, and high-temperature creep resistance. This necessitates further investigation into translating abstract physical mechanisms into concrete constraints or rules for XAI models, as well as integrating physical models across different scales (atomic, micro, and macro) with ML models. In addition, prediction uncertainty is quantified (e.g., using Bayesian optimization or integration methods) [ 498 ]. Uncertainty information can guide the experimental design, e.g., by selecting the most valuable experimental parameters and improving the model, e.g., by targeting regions of high uncertainty with finer modeling. Developing new uncertainty quantification methods, especially for small datasets and high-dimensional HEA data, is vital for enhancing model reliability and guiding experimental design.

sections.heading: Predict Processing-Structure–Property Relationships
paragraphs: High-quality databases containing processing parameters, microstructure, and performance data are essential for training reliable ML models. However, such data are still relatively scarce and of varying quality. In order to build researchers’ trust in ML models and guide experimental design, there is a need to further understand how ML models relate processing parameters to microstructure and performance, experimentally validate ML model predictions, and feed experimental results back into the model for improvement. Developing a closed-loop process from design and prediction to experimental validation is essential to accelerate the development of HEAs.

Extending ML models to include processing parameters (e.g., annealing temperatures and deformation rates) enables them to predict the final microstructures and properties, thus facilitating the optimization of the entire manufacturing process. Combining ML with additive-manufacturing (AM) techniques allows precise control of compositions and microstructures to produce complex HEA components with optimized performance. The RL strategy offers a promising approach for real-time control of AM, dynamically adjusting parameters (e.g., laser power, scan speed) based on feedback. RL can also autonomously learn and optimize, adapting to different materials and processes while improving defect detection and repair [ 499 ,  500 ]. Develop an inverse-design platform to create a closed-loop process from the design and prediction to experimental validation. Enable rapid screening and design of candidate HEA components based on target properties to guide experimental synthesis and characterization. For example, generative models (e.g., VAEs [ 501 ,  502 ], GANs [ 503 ]) can be utilized to generate candidate material compositions and processing parameters that satisfy the target properties. Combining HTC and experimental methods with inverse-design strategies can significantly accelerate the discovery and development of new materials. These strategies drive the HEA performance prediction toward greater accuracy, efficiency, and automation.

sections.heading: Conclusions
paragraphs: This review explores the entire process aspects of implementing ML methods to aid HEA design, aiming to guide researchers in using ML to accelerate the development of HEAs. It covers strategies for acquiring HEA data from different sources, such as computational simulations, experiments, and literature, and highlights the potential of the TM method in discovering novel HEAs. In addition, it explores techniques for expanding sparse HEA databases through data augmentation. The paper also discusses key issues, such as data quality, reliability, and sources of error in detail. Regarding feature engineering, standard-feature-filtering methods are presented alongside a focus on incorporating the domain knowledge to design novel descriptors with enhanced representational and predictive capabilities, thereby improving model accuracy and interpretability. This review systematically examines the application of a range of ML models in the HEA design, from classical algorithms, such as SVM, KNN, DTs, RF, GBDT, XGBoost, and LightGBM, to advanced deep-learning approaches. An evaluation of their advantages and disadvantages, as well as detailed examples of their applications and prediction results in the HEA research, is provided. The potential of semi-supervised learning and reinforcement learning for the HEA prediction is also explored.

Unlike previous reviews that primarily focused on the phase selection and mechanical-property prediction, the present work offers an in-depth analysis of the applications of ML models to predict the corrosion and oxidation resistance of HEAs, examining how ML can address the complex interplay of factors influencing these properties. Moreover, this review presents the current and future potential of learning strategies like AL, TL, inverse design, and QML for optimizing HEA-experimental design. It analyzes examples of existing model-interpretability methods and their limitations, aiming to accelerate the discovery of novel HEAs. Finally, the review summarizes existing findings and explores future research directions and challenges, offering a comprehensive roadmap for future research in the HEA field. Applying ML to HEAs is a rapidly evolving field with significant potential. Further research into developing and applying ML techniques holds great promise for accelerating the iterative design of novel HEAs with exceptional properties.
